It would require verification of biological sex by students’ healthcare providers. Should this measure be enacted into law?
items.summary: Washington schools must offer sports without regard to sex but may provide separate teams based on sex, and state guidelines prohibit discrimination based on sex and gender identity. Initiative 638 would, in its own language, prohibit “biologically male students from competing with and against female students” on teams or in events designated for female students only. The Attorney General says this would generally prevent transgender girls from participating on girls’ teams, and would cover public K-12 schools and private schools that participate in the Washington Interscholastic Activities Association or similar organizations. Students in female-only categories would need a form signed by their personal health care provider verifying “biological sex.”
items.yes: A yes vote would prohibit students defined as biologically male from competing in school sports intended for female students only, and would require healthcare provider verification of biological sex for those students.
items.no: A no vote would leave current Washington law and state guidelines in place, which prohibit discrimination in school sports based on sex and gender identity while allowing separate teams based on sex.

fiscal.text: The Office of Financial Management’s fiscal impact statement says the initiative would not affect state or local revenue. It estimates the Office of the Superintendent of Public Instruction would incur a one-time cost of approximately $21,000 to update guidelines, and that local school districts would likely incur costs to revise policies and procedures, but that this impact is indeterminate.

money.text: In reports Ballotpedia had processed through August 31, 2026, Let’s Go Washington, the committee supporting Initiative 638, reported $8,059,297.89 in total contributions. Ballotpedia notes the committee is funding three initiatives on the ballot (Initiatives 1, 638 and 645), so that total covers all three. The three committees registered to oppose it (No Hate in WA State, Defend Washington and Permanent Defense PAC) reported $3,843,631.74 in total contributions, a figure Ballotpedia lists on the pages for all three initiatives.

for.text: The official argument for says “Female athletes deserve fair opportunities to build confidence, develop skills, and pursue goals,” and that the measure would affirm Title IX’s recognition of “the necessity of the female category.” The rebuttal says “A female athlete should not lose a starting position, medal, championship, or college recruiting opportunity because the category created for her was not protected.”

It says the verification would be modest: “during a private, consented visit, a licensed medical professional would verify sex based on the student’s birth records, medical history and/or a standard, non-invasive physical examination.” The rebuttal says “IL26-638 doesn’t require invasive or expensive exams.”

It says the measure would align Washington with other bodies: “Federal law, the Women’s Tennis Association, World Athletics, and the International Olympic Committee have all adopted policies to protect eligibility for the female category.” The rebuttal cites “at least 269 placements by male athletes competing in girls’ interscholastic categories, including 74 firsts and 156 top-three finishes.”

against.text: The official argument against says the measure “would require girls as young as 8 to undergo intrusive medical sex certification as a new part of sports physicals” and “bans parents from using birth certificates.” It says “These requirements apply to girls only, boys are exempt.”

It says the Washington State Nurses Association, Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates and doctors warn the measure would subject girls to “medically unnecessary, embarrassing, and potentially harmful genital exams.” It says “Today, students remain fully clothed during sports physicals,” and that many girls without a regular family doctor would be examined by “total strangers.”

It says “This statewide blanket ban to kick 5 - 10 trans girls off school teams will negatively impact all girls, leaving no room for case by case decisions,” and that coaches and athletes say “invasive genital exam requirements” would discourage girls from playing sports.

unsaid.label: What the verification would require, according to the Attorney General.
unsaid.text: The explanatory statement says verification “would have to be based on the student’s reproductive anatomy, genetic makeup, or normal endogenously produced testosterone levels,” and concludes: “Students would thus have to undergo some type of medical evaluation of their sex to participate in interschool sports designated for female students only.” The pamphlet arguments disagree about how invasive that evaluation would be.
